Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue WordPress admin account created matching developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx · [LLM] Suspicious WordPress plugin folder created (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound traffic to tidio.cc or 84.201.6.54 (Awesome Motive supply-chain C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Outbound traffic to tidio.cc or 84.201.6.54 (Awesome Motive supply-chain C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects WordPress-hosting endpoints contacting the Sansec-published C2 destinations (tidio[.]cc and 84.201.6.54) used by the tampered PushEngage / OptinMonster / TrustPulse scripts to exfiltrate freshly-minted admin credentials and site metadata. Rationale: Sansec explicitly named tidio[.]cc (registered 2026-04-28) and 84.201.6.54 as the C2 destinations. Both are non-resolvable on a normal WordPress site, so direct IP/domain matches are high-fidelity. Time-bounded to the disclosure window to keep the alert tight. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain • https://www.pushengage.com/incident-report-june-2026/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher manually visiting tidio[.]cc for IOC validation from a workstation in scope
  • Threat-intel ingestion sandbox detonating the JS payload and replaying the callback
  • DNS resolver retry loop after the domain is sinkholed — duplicate DNS queries from the same host
  • Backup of historical pcap/web-proxy logs being re-indexed and triggering the same network rules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in ("84.201.6.54")
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the source host is a WordPress-hosting endpoint (web server or marketing site) and pull the initiating process / user-agent. Validate the connection was outbound (not inbound scan). 2. Contain — isolate the host, block tidio[.]cc and 84.201.6.54 at the egress proxy / DNS RPZ, and snapshot the wp-content/plugins tree before any cleanup. 3. Hunt — pivot on the host's web-server logs from June 12-14 UTC for inbound POSTs that match wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with previously-unseen action params; enumerate WordPress users for developer_api1 / dev_* and check wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper or database-optimizer folders.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["tidio.cc"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["84.201.6.54"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-21T00:00:00Z))
| where RemoteIP in (C2IPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
   or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)tidio\.cc(/|$)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["tidio.cc"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["84.201.6.54"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-21T00:00:00Z))
| where DestinationIP in (C2IPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, URL=RequestURL, DeviceVendor),
(DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-21T00:00:00Z))
| where Name has_any (C2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=ClientIP, DstHost=Name, QueryType, DeviceVendor="DNS"),
(ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-21T00:00:00Z))
| where DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstHost=DstHostname, URL=Url, DeviceVendor=EventVendor)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects outbound network connections to tidio.cc or 84.201.6.54 used by the PushEngage / OptinMonster / TrustPulse tampered-script campaign disclosed by Sansec in June 2026.

Tampered PushEngage SDK fetched from clientcdn.pushengage.com during exposure window AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for endpoints (or web servers acting as origin scrapers) that downloaded pushengage-web-sdk.js or pushengage-subscription.js from clientcdn.pushengage.com between 2026-06-12 and 2026-06-14 UTC, the window in which Sansec observed the tampered script being served. Rationale: The article (and PushEngage's own incident notice) name the two specific JS filenames and the exact CDN host. Bounding the search to 2026-06-12 → 2026-06-14 UTC matches the Sansec-published exposure window so legitimate post-cleanup loads do not trigger. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain • https://www.pushengage.com/incident-report-june-2026/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress site visitors who happened to load the SDK after the CDN cache was already cleared but before stale CDN edge nodes refreshed (PushEngage notes some servers still served it into June 14)
  • Web-scraping monitoring infra (Synthetics, Catchpoint) replaying the URL for availability checks
  • Security researchers downloading both filenames for analysis from corporate workstations
  • Internal CDN-cache invalidation tooling re-fetching the asset to populate replacement copies
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm whether the downloading endpoint is a WordPress admin browser session (high impact) versus a content-rendering visitor browser (low impact). Pull the SHA256 of the cached JS to compare to PushEngage's clean hash. 2. Contain — if an admin browser loaded the tampered file, force-logout all WordPress administrators on the affected site, rotate WP salts in wp-config.php, and invalidate session cookies. 3. Hunt — pivot to the C2 detection (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54) for the same DeviceId, enumerate users for developer_api1 or dev_xxxxxx, and inspect wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper or database-optimizer folders.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-14T23:59:59Z))
| where RemoteUrl has "clientcdn.pushengage.com"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js", "pushengage-subscription.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowStart = datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z);
let WindowEnd = datetime(2026-06-14T23:59:59Z);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated between (WindowStart .. WindowEnd)
| where (RequestURL has "clientcdn.pushengage.com") and (RequestURL has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, URL=RequestURL, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (WindowStart .. WindowEnd)
| where (Url has "clientcdn.pushengage.com") and (Url has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, URL=Url, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor=EventVendor),
(W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated between (WindowStart .. WindowEnd)
| where csUriStem has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=cIP, URL=strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), UserAgent=csUserAgent, DeviceVendor="IIS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue WordPress admin account created matching developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sansec-published rogue WordPress admin usernames (developer_api1 or anything matching dev_<6char>) appearing in identity / auth / web-server logs. The backdoor JS used the logged-in admin's session to create this account silently. Rationale: Sansec's IoC table explicitly lists 'developer_api1' and the pattern 'dev_xxxxxx' as the rogue admin usernames. These strings should not appear in any legitimate WordPress site's auth or web logs, making string-match detections high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer accounts coincidentally matching dev_<6char> naming (rare but possible at large hosting providers)
  • Threat-intel feeds / IOC ingestion pipelines emitting the username string in their own log lines
  • Security scanner (Wordfence, Sucuri) producing reports that include the rogue username for awareness
  • WordPress plugins that store the username verbatim in their changelog or admin notice
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the source site is one of the affected plugins (PushEngage, OptinMonster, TrustPulse) and pull the wp_users row for developer_api1 / matching dev_* accounts including user_registered timestamp. 2. Contain — delete the rogue admin account, rotate all administrator passwords + WP secret salts in wp-config.php, and invalidate active sessions via wp user session destroy --all. 3. Hunt — check wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper or database-optimizer directories, pivot to outbound traffic to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54, and rotate the CDN API key + database credentials.
union
(DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\wp-content\" or FolderPath has "/wp-content/"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("developer_api1", "dev_")),
(DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("developer_api1", "INSERT INTO wp_users", "wp_insert_user")
  and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)dev_[a-z0-9]{4,8}")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/wp-admin/user-new.php","/wp-admin/users.php","/wp-json/wp/v2/users","/xmlrpc.php")
| where csUriQuery has_any ("developer_api1","dev_") or csUriStem has "developer_api1"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=cIP, URL=strcat(csUriStem,"?",csUriQuery), Method=csMethod, UA=csUserAgent),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("developer_api1","wp_insert_user")
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)\bdev_[a-z0-9]{4,8}\b"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, ProcessName, Message=SyslogMessage),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("developer_api1","/wp-json/wp/v2/users","/wp-admin/user-new.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, URL=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rogue WordPress admin account developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx
id: 4b2e7c8e-2f1a-4f3b-9c2a-8e7d4b1c5f02
description: Detects creation of, or web-app references to, the Sansec-published rogue WordPress admin usernames (developer_api1, dev_xxxxxx) planted by the tampered PushEngage / OptinMonster / TrustPulse scripts.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1136.001
  - attack.t1098
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_user:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'developer_api1'
      - 'dev_'
  selection_endpoint:
    c-uri|contains:
      - '/wp-admin/user-new.php'
      - '/wp-json/wp/v2/users'
      - '/wp-admin/users.php'
  condition: selection_user and selection_endpoint
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:syslog) AND (@http.url:(*\/wp-admin\/user-new.php* OR *\/wp-json\/wp\/v2\/users*) OR @message:*wp_insert_user*) AND (@http.url:*developer_api1* OR @message:*developer_api1* OR @message:/dev_[a-z0-9]{4,8}/)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (CommandLine=/developer_api1/i OR CommandLine=/dev_[a-z0-9]{4,8}/i OR CommandLine=/wp_insert_user/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.src) as src values(All_Changes.action) as action from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="user" AND (All_Changes.user="developer_api1" OR All_Changes.user="dev_*") by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*wp-admin/user-new.php*" OR Web.url="*wp-json/wp/v2/users*") AND (Web.url="*developer_api1*" OR Web.url="*dev_*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.src) as src values(All_Changes.action) as action from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="user" AND (All_Changes.user="developer_api1" OR All_Changes.user="dev_*") by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*wp-admin/user-new.php*" OR Web.url="*wp-json/wp/v2/users*") AND (Web.url="*developer_api1*" OR Web.url="*dev_*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Suspicious WordPress plugin folder created (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the Sansec-named hidden-plugin directories that the backdoor installs under wp-content/plugins. These plugin folder names are not associated with any legitimate WordPress plugin and represent the in-tree web shell. Rationale: The article quotes Sansec's IOC list naming exactly two backdoor plugin folders: content-delivery-helper ('Content Delivery Helper') and database-optimizer ('Database Optimizer'). Neither matches any plugin in the WordPress.org repository, so file-create events under those subpaths are nearly noise-free. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic analyst extracting a tarball of the compromised plugin folder onto a sandbox host for analysis
  • Backup-restore process replaying historical file events into the SIEM after a clean-up
  • Custom internal plugin coincidentally named 'database-optimizer' in a hosting provider's site template (rare — verify by SHA256 against known-good hashes)
  • Wordfence / Sucuri scanner quarantining the backdoor and producing its own file-event records
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the host is a WordPress web server and the directory path actually exists on disk. Capture file listing + SHA256 of the PHP files in those folders. 2. Contain — quarantine the entire wp-content/plugins/<folder>/ directory tree (do not delete; preserve for forensics), block the host's egress to tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54, and disable the wp-admin endpoint pending review. 3. Hunt — enumerate wp_users for developer_api1 / dev_* accounts, search for any other PHP files modified in the same minute window across wp-content, and check web-server access logs for the web-shell URL by correlating against subsequent outbound POSTs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]wp-content[\\/]plugins[\\/](content-delivery-helper|database-optimizer)[\\/]"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let Suspicious = dynamic(["content-delivery-helper","database-optimizer"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]wp-content[\\/]plugins[\\/](content-delivery-helper|database-optimizer)[\\/]"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=ActorUsername, FilePath=TargetFilePath, Process=ActingProcessName, Cmd=ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash=TargetFileSHA256),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any (Suspicious) and SyslogMessage has "wp-content/plugins/"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, Actor="", FilePath=SyslogMessage, Process=ProcessName, Cmd="", Hash="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sansec hidden WordPress plugin directory (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer)
id: 7c4d5e6f-3a2b-4c7d-9e1f-2b3a4c5d6e03
description: Detects creation of the hidden-plugin directories installed by the tampered PushEngage / OptinMonster / TrustPulse scripts (Sansec, June 2026). These directories carry the web shell that does not surface in the WordPress dashboard.

WordPress PHP process spawning shell from wp-content directory AIExploitation Medium
Detects php / php-fpm / php-cgi processes whose working directory or invoking script path resolves under wp-content spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe / bash / sh — the canonical web-shell execution shape for the hidden Sansec backdoor. Rationale: The article says the hidden plugin opens a web shell — 'anyone who knows the right URL can run code on the server.' On a WordPress host, that materialises as php / php-fpm spawning a shell or curl/wget. Anchoring on the wp-content / wp-admin path eliminates generic PHP CLI scripts. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress CLI tools (wp-cli) running maintenance tasks that legitimately spawn curl for plugin updates
  • Backup plugins (UpdraftPlus, BackupBuddy) shelling out to tar/gzip from wp-content/uploads
  • Image-processing plugins invoking imagemagick / ffmpeg via shell wrappers
  • Cron-scheduled WordPress jobs that pull remote feeds via curl from wp-content paths
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","updraftplus","backupbuddy","wp-cron.php") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tar","gzip","rsync"))
Response runbook
1. Triage — capture the full process chain (grandparent → parent → child) and the script path resolved from the PHP CLI args. Identify which WordPress plugin owns the parent path. 2. Contain — kill the offending PHP worker, quarantine the parent script file, and add a temporary egress block for the host to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54. 3. Hunt — pivot on the same DeviceId for content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer folder writes, rogue developer_api1 / dev_* admin accounts, and inbound HTTP requests for the script path in web-server access logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d", "FromBase64String", "eval(", "system(", "passthru(")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin","wp-includes")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])php(-cgi|-fpm)?(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|bash|sh|dash|zsh|nc|ncat|curl(\.exe)?|wget(\.exe)?)$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d","FromBase64String","eval(","system(","passthru(")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin","wp-includes")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=ActorUsername,
          Parent=ParentProcessName, ParentCmd=ParentProcessCommandLine,
          Child=ActingProcessName, ChildCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PHP process spawning shell from WordPress directory
id: 8e5d6f7a-4b3c-4d8e-9a2f-3c4d5e6f7a04
description: Detects php / php-fpm / php-cgi spawning a shell or download utility while running with wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes in its path or command line — the canonical Sansec backdoor web-shell execution pattern.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php'
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php-cgi'
      - '\php.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
  selection_path:

      - 'wp-content'
      - 'wp-admin'
      - 'wp-includes'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_path
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) AND @ParentImage:(*\php.exe OR *\PHP.EXE OR */php OR */php-fpm OR */php-cgi) AND @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR */bash OR */sh OR */dash OR */curl OR */wget OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe) AND @ParentCommandLine:(*wp-content* OR *wp-admin* OR *wp-includes*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^php(-cgi|-fpm)?(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|[\\\/](bash|sh|dash|zsh|nc|ncat|curl|wget))(\.exe)?$/i

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EvilTokens lure email - inbound message referencing microsoft.com/devicelogin or device code prompts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Successful Entra ID device code OAuth flow sign-in - EvilTokens authorisation handoff · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Host or user contacting EvilTokens C2 / lure infrastructure (IOC sweep) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inbox rule creation immediately following Entra ID device code sign-in · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
EvilTokens lure email - inbound message referencing microsoft.com/devicelogin or device code prompts AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails carrying EvilTokens phishing lures: messages whose URLs or subject lines reference microsoft.com/devicelogin, 'verify to view' or 'signature required' wording typical of the kit's decoy pages. Article-specific because EvilTokens directs victims to enter the attacker's code at the real Microsoft device login portal. Rationale: Subject wording 'Verify to view' / 'Signature required' and the destination microsoft.com/devicelogin are directly quoted from the article body. Lure-host domains taken from pre-extracted IOC list. Sentinel falls back to OfficeActivity since EmailEvents is a Defender-XDR table not guaranteed in every Sentinel tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-block-authentication-flows
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT communications instructing users to activate a new Teams Room or conference-room device via device code
  • Microsoft service notifications referencing devicelogin for setup of Outlook on a new machine
  • DocuSign / Adobe Sign legitimate 'Signature required' notifications
  • Internal phishing-simulation campaigns using the same lure wording
  • Vendor SharePoint share notifications with 'shared document' subject phrasing
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("microsoft.com","docusign.net","adobesign.com") and SenderFromAddress !endswith "@yourorg.com"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full message via EmailEvents.NetworkMessageId, compare SenderFromAddress vs SenderMailFromAddress for spoofing, review SPF/DKIM/DMARC, and check UrlClickEvents for whether any recipient actually clicked. Contain: ZAP-purge the message for all recipients, block the sender domain at the gateway, and tenant-block the lure URL. If any recipient clicked, immediately revoke their Entra sessions, invalidate refresh tokens, and reset MFA. Hunt: pivot on RecipientEmailAddress into SigninLogs over the next 24h looking for successful deviceCode authentications; if found, escalate to the EvilTokens account-takeover playbook and audit for new inbox rules + OAuth app consents.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("verify to view","signature required","device code","devicelogin","shared document","signature requested")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where Url has_any ("microsoft.com/devicelogin","oauth2/deviceauth","authdocspro.com","backdoor-hub.com","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","notificationsmanagersec.com","internalmemorecord.bxwancheng.com","newmobilepolojean.com")
) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("Send","MailItemsAccessed","Create")
| where Subject has_any ("verify to view","signature required","device code","devicelogin","shared document")
   or Parameters has_any ("microsoft.com/devicelogin","authdocspro.com","notificationsmanagersec.com","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","backdoor-hub.com","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, Subject, UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Successful Entra ID device code OAuth flow sign-in - EvilTokens authorisation handoff AIExploitation High
Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant. EvilTokens abuses this exact flow: the attacker requests a device code, the victim authenticates it on microsoft.com/devicelogin, and Microsoft issues access + refresh tokens to the attacker's session. Device code auth is rare in normal corporate use, making any success a high-fidelity hunt pivot. Rationale: Article states EvilTokens 'abuses the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow' and that 'Microsoft issues access and refresh tokens to the session opened by the attacker'. Successful deviceCode auth is rare in normal enterprise use, so a clean match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked with Sekoia and Microsoft device-code-flow Conditional Access guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-block-authentication-flows • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004 T1566
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Teams Room / Surface Hub / conference-room device enrollment using device code flow
  • Help-desk-assisted sign-in to an Azure VM via Azure CLI device code
  • Developer / sysadmin using 'az login --use-device-code' on a remote host
  • First-time setup of legitimate IoT devices (digital signage, printers) against the tenant
  • PowerShell automation using Microsoft Graph SDK device code authentication during migrations
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Teams Rooms","Surface Hub","Azure CLI") and DeviceDetail !has "Teams Room"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the SigninLogs entry for the request, check IPAddress geolocation and ASN against the user's normal pattern, identify the AppDisplayName (Microsoft Graph / Azure CLI / Office Apps are most-abused), and search for the preceding EvilTokens lure email to the same UPN. Contain: immediately revoke the user's sessions via Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken, invalidate refresh tokens via Graph API, force password reset and MFA re-registration. Hunt: search OfficeActivity for inbox-rule creation, mailbox-forwarding setup, and mass-download events within 24h of the sign-in; review OAuth consent grants for the affected UPN; pivot on the source IP across all tenant sign-ins for additional victims.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| extend AuthProcessingStr = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthProcessingStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, AppDisplayName, ApplicationId, UserAgent, DeviceName, AadDeviceId, IsAnonymousProxy, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState, ConditionalAccessStatus, AuthDetailsStr
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| extend AuthProcessingStr = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthProcessingStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceDetail, AutonomousSystemNumber, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState, ConditionalAccessStatus, OriginalRequestId, AuthDetailsStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Successful Entra ID Device Code OAuth Sign-In

description: Detects a successful Microsoft Entra ID sign-in that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant. Abused by EvilTokens to obtain tokens without phishing the password.

Host or user contacting EvilTokens C2 / lure infrastructure (IOC sweep) AICommand & Control Medium
Sweeps network/DNS telemetry for outbound contact to EvilTokens phishing/C2 IPs and domains from the article's IOC list. Article-specific because these are exactly the indicators tied to the kit's active campaigns since February 2026, including the March 2026 campaign hitting 340+ organisations. Rationale: All IPs and domains are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC list, tied to EvilTokens campaigns documented by Sekoia and Microsoft Threat Intel. Sweep covers both initial lure-page contact and any post-tokenization C2/redirector traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing / SaaS traffic if any listed domain is later reclaimed by a benign owner
  • Security researchers / sandbox detonation environments inside the org browsing IOC URLs intentionally
  • Proxy/inspection-bypass services briefly resolving the domains as part of TI feed enrichment
  • Email security gateways pre-rendering URLs in inbound mail (URL detonation rather than user click)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the initiating process and user (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn / ContextImageFileName) — browser is expected for lure-page hits, anything else is more concerning. Cross-reference with EmailEvents to find the originating message and with SigninLogs for any device code success in the next 60 minutes. Contain: block the indicators at the proxy/firewall/DNS layer, isolate the host if a non-browser process generated the hit, and force session revocation + token invalidation for the involved user. Hunt: expand IOC pivot by 30 days, look for newly registered look-alike domains on the same name servers, query OAuth consent grants and inbox rules for the user, and submit the indicators to internal TI for cross-tenant sweep.
let EvilTokensDomains = dynamic(["authdocspro.com","backdoor-hub.com","bumpgames.net","carbatterygurgaon.com","careldutoit-el.co.za","dao.com.au","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com","eqfit.co.za","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","internalmemorecord.bxwancheng.com","macmamo.com","mirsanotolastik.com","mirzanyapi.com","newmobilepolojean.com","notificationsmanagersec.com","pelangiservice.com","prcservis.com"]);
let EvilTokensIPs = dynamic(["162.220.232.0","162.220.234.0","89.150.45.0","185.81.113.0"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in (EvilTokensIPs) 
   or RemoteUrl has_any (EvilTokensDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol

let EvilTokensIPs = dynamic(["162.220.232.0","162.220.234.0","89.150.45.0","185.81.113.0"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DestinationIP in (EvilTokensIPs) or RequestURL has_any (EvilTokensDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (EvilTokensDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct),
(DnsEvents

  | where Name has_any (EvilTokensDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

(@network.destination.ip:(162.220.232.0 OR 162.220.234.0 OR 89.150.45.0 OR 185.81.113.0) OR @dns.question.name:(authdocspro.com OR backdoor-hub.com OR eventcalender-schedule.com OR evobothub.org OR framebound.cloud OR infinitechai.org OR notificationsmanagersec.com OR docusend.networkssolutionmail.com OR internalmemorecord.bxwancheng.com OR newmobilepolojean.com OR bumpgames.net OR macmamo.com OR mirsanotolastik.com OR mirzanyapi.com OR pelangiservice.com OR prcservis.com OR carbatterygurgaon.com OR "careldutoit-el.co.za" OR "dao.com.au" OR "eqfit.co.za") OR @url.domain:(authdocspro.com OR backdoor-hub.com OR eventcalender-schedule.com OR evobothub.org OR framebound.cloud OR infinitechai.org OR notificationsmanagersec.com))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^(authdocspro\.com|backdoor-hub\.com|eventcalender-schedule\.com|evobothub\.org|framebound\.cloud|infinitechai\.org|notificationsmanagersec\.com|docusend\.networkssolutionmail\.com|internalmemorecord\.bxwancheng\.com|newmobilepolojean\.com|bumpgames\.net|macmamo\.com|mirsanotolastik\.com|mirzanyapi\.com|pelangiservice\.com|prcservis\.com|carbatterygurgaon\.com|careldutoit-el\.co\.za|dao\.com\.au|eqfit\.co\.za)$/i)
OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(162\.220\.232\.0|162\.220\.234\.0|89\.150\.45\.0|185\.81\.113\.0)$/)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest in ("162.220.232.0","162.220.234.0","89.150.45.0","185.81.113.0") OR Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest_host IN ("authdocspro.com","backdoor-hub.com","bumpgames.net","carbatterygurgaon.com","careldutoit-el.co.za","dao.com.au","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com","eqfit.co.za","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","internalmemorecord.bxwancheng.com","macmamo.com","mirsanotolastik.com","mirzanyapi.com","newmobilepolojean.com","notificationsmanagersec.com","pelangiservice.com","prcservis.com")) by Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.src Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest_host Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name("Network_Traffic.All_Traffic")` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest in ("162.220.232.0","162.220.234.0","89.150.45.0","185.81.113.0") OR Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest_host IN ("authdocspro.com","backdoor-hub.com","bumpgames.net","carbatterygurgaon.com","careldutoit-el.co.za","dao.com.au","docusend.networkssolutionmail.com","eqfit.co.za","eventcalender-schedule.com","evobothub.org","framebound.cloud","infinitechai.org","internalmemorecord.bxwancheng.com","macmamo.com","mirsanotolastik.com","mirzanyapi.com","newmobilepolojean.com","notificationsmanagersec.com","pelangiservice.com","prcservis.com")) by Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.src Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.dest_host Network_Traffic.All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name("Network_Traffic.All_Traffic")` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Inbox rule creation immediately following Entra ID device code sign-in AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a successful Entra ID deviceCode sign-in with the creation of a new mailbox inbox rule for the same user within 60 minutes. EvilTokens operators routinely set hide/forward/delete rules post-tokenization to stage BEC against finance, HR, logistics and sales mailboxes — this combination is the article's specific post-compromise tell. Rationale: Article explicitly warns to 'watch for unusual device-code authentication ... and new inbox rules' and ties post-tokenization actions to BEC preparation against finance/HR/logistics/sales mailboxes. The 60-minute join window encodes that the inbox rule is part of the same takeover session. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User self-service Outlook rules created shortly after a legitimate Surface Hub / Teams Room device code authentication
  • Migration scripts using device code auth to programmatically configure inbox rules for users
  • Sysadmin re-provisioning an account via Microsoft Graph SDK device code login
  • Anti-spam / mailbox-cleanup vendor tooling that authenticates via device code and configures rules
  • Legitimate executive assistant configuring rules on a delegated mailbox right after sign-in
Suppression filter
| where Parameters !has "Stop-Processing" and AppDisplayName !in~ ("Outlook Web App","Microsoft Office")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full inbox rule JSON from Parameters/RawEventData — hide/forward/delete rules with single-character names or names like '. ' / '!' are textbook EvilTokens BEC staging. Identify the source IP and ASN of the device code sign-in. Contain: revoke all sessions and refresh tokens for the user (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken + Disconnect-MgGraph), disable the malicious inbox rule via Remove-InboxRule, and reset the account password and MFA registration. Hunt: search the user's mailbox for sent items in the rule window for outbound BEC attempts, audit other Entra users for the same source IP, and run a 30-day OfficeActivity sweep for matching rule patterns across the tenant.
let DeviceCodeSignIns = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
    | where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
    | project DeviceCodeTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Application;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend RuleDetails = tostring(RawEventData)
| where RuleDetails has_any ("DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","MarkAsRead")
   or RuleDetails has_any ("RSS Feeds","Archive","Conversation History",".. ","!")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeSignIns on $left.AccountDisplayName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (DeviceCodeTime .. DeviceCodeTime + 60m)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, DeviceCodeTime)
| project DeviceCodeTime, RuleCreatedTime = Timestamp, DelayMinutes, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Application, ActionType, ObjectName, RuleDetails
| order by RuleCreatedTime desc
let DeviceCodeSignIns = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | extend AuthDetailsStr = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
    | where AuthDetailsStr has "deviceCode" or AuthenticationRequirement has "deviceCode"
    | project DeviceCodeTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName), IPAddress, AppDisplayName, OriginalRequestId;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserId)
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","MarkAsRead")
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeSignIns on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (DeviceCodeTime .. DeviceCodeTime + 60m)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, DeviceCodeTime)
| project DeviceCodeTime, RuleCreatedTime = TimeGenerated, DelayMinutes, UserPrincipalName, ClientIP, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Operation, Parameters
| order by RuleCreatedTime desc
source:office365 @evt.name:("New-InboxRule" OR "Set-InboxRule" OR "UpdateInboxRules") @Parameters:(*DeleteMessage* OR *MoveToFolder* OR *ForwardTo* OR *RedirectTo*)
CLOUD

| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as deviceCodeTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.signature="deviceCode" by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | join type=inner user [ | tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as ruleTime from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created Change.object_category="InboxRule" by Change.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | rename Change.user as user ] | eval diff_sec=ruleTime-deviceCodeTime | where diff_sec>=0 AND diff_sec<=3600 | convert ctime(deviceCodeTime) ctime(ruleTime)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    category: process_creation

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

Sniper Dz Scams Target MENA Users via Fake Facebook Offers and Browser Alerts

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of fraudulent activity targeting users across the Middle East and North Africa by employing various fraudulent Facebook accounts impersonating politicians, public figures, and trusted organizations. "These accounts promoted fake offers, including free mobile internet packages, financial compensation, and government subsidy programs," Group-IB

ATT&CKT1190 T1555.003 T1566

IPs65.60.9.236 108.178.23.118 184.154.10.254
